<script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w19">{"year":1,"week":19,"id":"y1w19","title":"Measurement, Perimeter and Area of Plane Shapes","subtitle":"Referents and units; converting units of length and area; perimeter; areas of rectangles, triangles, parallelograms, trapeziums and circles; composite and irregular shapes; costing problems.","family":"geometry","section":{"no":3,"name":"Geometry and Measurement","strand":"Geometry Around Us","from":13,"to":20},"outcomes":["Use sensible referents to estimate lengths and areas, and convert between units of length and area.","Calculate the perimeter and area of common plane shapes, including circles.","Find the area of composite shapes by adding and subtracting parts, and estimate irregular areas on a grid.","Solve fencing, flooring, tiling and painting problems, including costs.","Explain how the area changes when lengths are scaled."],"keywords":["referent","unit conversion","perimeter","circumference","area","square unit","hectare","composite shape","annulus","estimate","scale factor"],"notes":[{"title":"What measurement means","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"To **measure** is to compare a quantity with an agreed unit. A **referent** is a familiar object used to estimate a size: a classroom door is about 1 m wide, and a square 1 m by 1 m has an area of 1 m². A referent gives an **estimate**; use a ruler or tape when you need accuracy."},{"k":"ul","items":["**Length** is a distance in one direction (m, cm, km).","**Perimeter** is the distance all the way round a shape (also a length).","**Area** is the amount of surface inside a boundary (m², cm², hectares)."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Converting units","blocks":[{"k":"table","head":["Length","Area"],"rows":[["$1$ km $=1000$ m","$1$ km² $=1\\,000\\,000$ m²"],["$1$ m $=100$ cm","$1$ m² $=10\\,000$ cm²"],["$1$ cm $=10$ mm","$1$ cm² $=100$ mm²"],["$1$ inch $=2.54$ cm","$1$ hectare (ha) $=10\\,000$ m²"]]},{"k":"fig","id":"w19-units","caption":"A square metre is 100 cm by 100 cm, so it contains $100\\times100=10\\,000$ square centimetres."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Square the conversion factor for area","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Since $1$ m $=100$ cm, $1$ m² $=100^2$ cm² $=10\\,000$ cm². So $4800$ cm² $=0.48$ m², **not** $48$ m². This matters when you buy tiles or paint."}]}],"figs":["w19-units"]},{"title":"Perimeter","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The perimeter is the total length of the boundary, given in units of length (m, cm)."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Perimeters","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Rectangle: $P=2(l+b)$","Square: $P=4a$","Triangle: $P=a+b+c$","Circle (circumference): $C=2\\pi r=\\pi d$"]}]},{"k":"p","text":"For a composite shape, walk round the **outside** only; do not add the lines inside the shape."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Areas of common shapes","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Area is given in **square units**. The height $h$ is always measured **at right angles** (perpendicular) to the base."},{"k":"fig","id":"w19-shapes","caption":"The area formulas. The dashed lines show the perpendicular heights."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Areas","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Rectangle: $A=lb$; $\\;$ square: $A=a^2$","Triangle: $A=\\tfrac{1}{2}bh$","Parallelogram: $A=bh$","Trapezium: $A=\\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b)h$, where $a$ and $b$ are the parallel sides","Circle: $A=\\pi r^2$"]}]}],"figs":["w19-shapes"]},{"title":"Composite and irregular shapes","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **composite** shape is made of simpler shapes. Mark all the lengths, split the shape with a dividing line, find each area, then **add** the parts. If a piece has been cut out, **subtract** its area."},{"k":"fig","id":"w19-lshape","caption":"The L-shape is a $16\\times12$ rectangle with a $6\\times5$ corner removed: $192-30=162$ m²."},{"k":"p","text":"An **annulus** (ring) is the region between two circles with the same centre: $A=\\pi R^2-\\pi r^2=\\pi(R^2-r^2)$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w19-annulus","caption":"The walkway is the outer circle minus the pond."},{"k":"p","text":"**Irregular shapes** drawn on squared paper can be estimated: count the whole squares, and count each part square as about half."},{"k":"fig","id":"w19-grid","caption":"Whole squares count 1; part squares count about $\\frac{1}{2}$ each. The answer is an estimate."}],"figs":["w19-lshape","w19-annulus","w19-grid"]},{"title":"Costing and measurement decisions","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Fencing, edging and wire** depend on the **perimeter**.","**Tiles, paint, roofing and carpet** depend on the **area**."]},{"k":"p","text":"Change all lengths to the same unit before you calculate. Allow for gates, waste, overlaps or several coats of paint if the question says so. Round the number of tiles, tins or packets **up**, because you cannot buy part of one."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Scaling a shape","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"If every length of a shape is multiplied by $k$, the perimeter is multiplied by $k$ but the area is multiplied by $k^2$. Doubling the sides of a rectangle multiplies its area by $4$."}]},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Check your answers","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Sketch the shape and label it. Check that perimeters are in m (or cm) and areas in m² (or cm²). Compare the answer with a simple rectangle that is a little larger. If $\\pi$ is not given, use the $\\pi$ key or $3.142$ and say which you used."}]}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"Fencing a garden","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A rectangular school garden measures 28 m by 17 m. A 3 m gate is left unfenced. Find (a) the length of wire for one round of fencing, (b) the cost at GH₵42 per metre."}],"steps":["Perimeter: $P=2(28+17)=2\\times45=90$ m.","Leave out the gate: $90-3=87$ m.","Cost: $87\\times42=3654$."],"answer":"(a) 87 m (b) GH₵3,654","figs":[]},{"title":"Tiling a hall","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A hall floor measures 7.5 m by 6.4 m. Square tiles have sides of 40 cm. Ignoring waste, how many tiles are needed?"}],"steps":["Floor area: $7.5\\times6.4=48$ m².","Tile side: $40$ cm $=0.40$ m, so one tile covers $0.40\\times0.40=0.16$ m².","Number of tiles: $48\\div0.16=300$."],"answer":"300 tiles","figs":[]},{"title":"A rectangle with a semicircle","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A courtyard is a 20 m by 12 m rectangle with a semicircle of radius 6 m on one of the 12 m sides. Find the total area in terms of $\\pi$."}],"steps":["Rectangle: $20\\times12=240$ m².","Semicircle: $\\tfrac{1}{2}\\pi r^2=\\tfrac{1}{2}\\pi(6^2)=18\\pi$ m².","The parts do not overlap, so add them."],"answer":"$(240+18\\pi)$ m²","figs":[]},{"title":"A trapezium-shaped plot","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A plot is a trapezium with parallel sides 24 m and 38 m, which are 15 m apart. Find its area and the cost of clearing it at GH₵8.50 per m²."}],"steps":["$A=\\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b)h=\\tfrac{1}{2}(24+38)\\times15=\\tfrac{1}{2}\\times62\\times15=465$ m².","Cost: $465\\times8.50=3952.50$."],"answer":"465 m²; GH₵3,952.50","figs":[]},{"title":"An L-shaped compound","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"An L-shaped compound is a 16 m by 12 m rectangle with a 6 m by 5 m rectangle removed from one corner. Find its area and its perimeter."}],"steps":["Full rectangle: $16\\times12=192$ m². Corner: $6\\times5=30$ m².","Area: $192-30=162$ m².","Removing the corner replaces two edges (6 m and 5 m) with two equal edges (5 m and 6 m) set inwards, so the perimeter does not change: $2(16+12)=56$ m."],"answer":"Area 162 m²; perimeter 56 m.","figs":[]},{"title":"A walkway round a pond","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A circular pond has a diameter of 14 m. A walkway 2 m wide surrounds it. Find the area of the walkway, using $\\pi=\\dfrac{22}{7}$."}],"steps":["Inner radius $=7$ m; outer radius $=7+2=9$ m.","Walkway $=\\pi(9^2-7^2)=\\pi(81-49)=32\\pi$.","$32\\times\\dfrac{22}{7}=\\dfrac{704}{7}\\approx100.57$."],"answer":"About 100.57 m²","figs":[]},{"title":"Painting a board","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A triangular board has a base of 3.2 m and a perpendicular height of 1.75 m. It needs two coats of paint, and 1 litre covers 4 m² in one coat. How many whole litres must be bought?"}],"steps":["Area: $\\tfrac{1}{2}\\times3.2\\times1.75=2.8$ m².","Two coats: $2\\times2.8=5.6$ m².","Paint: $5.6\\div4=1.4$ litres.","Paint is sold in whole litres, so round **up**."],"answer":"2 litres","figs":[]},{"title":"Area in hectares","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A rectangular field is 0.08 km long and 75 m wide. Find its area in hectares and its perimeter in metres."}],"steps":["Same units: $0.08$ km $=80$ m.","Area: $80\\times75=6000$ m² $=6000\\div10\\,000=0.6$ ha.","Perimeter: $2(80+75)=310$ m."],"answer":"0.6 ha; 310 m","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results for Week 19","items":["$1$ m² $=10\\,000$ cm²; $\\;1$ ha $=10\\,000$ m².","Rectangle $A=lb$, $P=2(l+b)$; triangle $A=\\tfrac{1}{2}bh$; parallelogram $A=bh$.","Trapezium $A=\\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b)h$; circle $A=\\pi r^2$, $C=2\\pi r$.","Annulus $A=\\pi(R^2-r^2)$.","Fencing uses perimeter; tiling and painting use area. Round whole items up."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"A room measures 8 m by 5 m. What is its perimeter?","options":["13 m","26 m","40 m","80 m"],"correct":1,"explain":"$P=2(8+5)=26$ m."},{"q":"Which is equal to 2.5 m²?","options":["250 cm²","2 500 cm²","25 000 cm²","250 000 cm²"],"correct":2,"explain":"$1$ m² $=10\\,000$ cm², so $2.5$ m² $=25\\,000$ cm²."},{"q":"A triangle has a base of 14 cm and a perpendicular height of 9 cm. Find its area.","options":["63 cm²","126 cm²","23 cm²","46 cm²"],"correct":0,"explain":"$A=\\tfrac{1}{2}\\times14\\times9=63$ cm²."},{"q":"A circular pond has a radius of 4 m. What is its area?","options":["$8\\pi$ m²","$12\\pi$ m²","$16\\pi$ m²","$32\\pi$ m²"],"correct":2,"explain":"$A=\\pi r^2=\\pi\\times4^2=16\\pi$ m²."},{"q":"A 12 m by 9 m courtyard has a 3 m by 4 m flower bed. Find the area that is not flower bed.","options":["96 m²","108 m²","120 m²","84 m²"],"correct":0,"explain":"$108-12=96$ m²."},{"q":"How many 25 cm by 20 cm tiles cover 10 m², ignoring waste?","options":["20","50","100","200"],"correct":3,"explain":"One tile covers $0.25\\times0.20=0.05$ m², and $10\\div0.05=200$."},{"q":"Which quantity tells you how much fencing wire is needed?","options":["area","volume","perimeter","capacity"],"correct":2,"explain":"Fencing goes round the boundary."},{"q":"A trapezium has parallel sides 8 cm and 12 cm and a height of 5 cm. Its area is","options":["50 cm²","100 cm²","40 cm²","25 cm²"],"correct":0,"explain":"$A=\\tfrac{1}{2}(8+12)\\times5=50$ cm²."},{"q":"A square has an area of 81 m². Find its perimeter.","options":["18 m","36 m","9 m","162 m"],"correct":1,"explain":"Side $=\\sqrt{81}=9$ m; perimeter $=4\\times9=36$ m."},{"q":"Both the length and the breadth of a rectangle are doubled. What happens to the area?","options":["It does not change.","It doubles.","It is multiplied by 4.","It halves."],"correct":2,"explain":"$(2l)(2b)=4lb$."}],"exercise":[{"q":"A 35 m by 24 m plot has one 4 m gate. Find the length of wire needed for three strands of fencing.","a":"$P=2(35+24)=118$ m; $118-4=114$ m; $3\\times114=342$ m."},{"q":"A ring has an outer radius of 9 cm and an inner radius of 5 cm. Find its area in terms of $\\pi$.","a":"$\\pi(81-25)=56\\pi$ cm²"},{"q":"Write 4.8 hectares in m² and in km².","a":"$48\\,000$ m² $=0.048$ km²"},{"q":"Give two rectangles with area 72 m² but different perimeters. What does this show?","a":"e.g. $8\\times9$ ($P=34$ m) and $6\\times12$ ($P=36$ m). Equal areas do not mean equal perimeters."},{"q":"A 16 m by 9 m compound has a circular pond of radius 2 m that is not paved. Find the paved area and the cost of paving at GH₵135 per m².","a":"$144-4\\pi\\approx131.43$ m²; cost $\\approx$ GH₵17,743.54."},{"q":"Find the circumference and the area of a circle of radius 7 cm, using $\\pi=\\dfrac{22}{7}$.","a":"$C=2\\times\\dfrac{22}{7}\\times7=44$ cm; $A=\\dfrac{22}{7}\\times49=154$ cm²."},{"q":"Find the area of a parallelogram with base 12 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm.","a":"$12\\times7=84$ cm²"},{"q":"A circle has a circumference of 31.4 m. Using $\\pi=3.14$, find its radius and area.","a":"$r=\\dfrac{31.4}{2\\times3.14}=5$ m; $A=3.14\\times25=78.5$ m²."}],"theory":[{"q":"Explain the difference between perimeter and area, using a rectangular vegetable bed 10 m by 6 m.","steps":["Perimeter is the length of the boundary, in metres: $P=2(10+6)=32$ m. It tells you how much fencing is needed.","Area is the surface inside, in square metres: $A=10\\times6=60$ m². It tells you how much ground can be planted."],"answer":"$P=32$ m (a length); $A=60$ m² (a surface).","model":null},{"q":"A rectangle has a perimeter of 58 m and one side of 12 m. Find the other side and the area.","steps":["$2(l+12)=58$, so $l+12=29$ and $l=17$ m.","Area $=17\\times12=204$ m²."],"answer":"17 m; 204 m²","model":null},{"q":"Explain how to change 3.6 m² into cm².","steps":["$1$ m $=100$ cm, so $1$ m² $=100\\times100=10\\,000$ cm².","$3.6$ m² $=3.6\\times10\\,000=36\\,000$ cm²."],"answer":"$36\\,000$ cm²","model":null},{"q":"A ring (annulus) has radii 10 cm and 6 cm. Find its area and explain why you subtract.","steps":["The ring is the large circle with the small circle removed.","$A=\\pi(10^2-6^2)=\\pi(100-36)=64\\pi$ cm²."],"answer":"$64\\pi\\approx201.1$ cm²","model":null},{"q":"A farmer increases both the length and the breadth of a rectangular plot by $20\\%$. Explain what happens to the perimeter and the area.","steps":["Each side is multiplied by $1.2$, so the perimeter is multiplied by $1.2$: a $20\\%$ increase.","The area is multiplied by $1.2\\times1.2=1.44$: a $44\\%$ increase."],"answer":"Perimeter $+20\\%$; area $+44\\%$.","model":null}],"checklist":["I can convert units of length and area, squaring the factor for area.","I can <script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w20">{"year":1,"week":20,"id":"y1w20","title":"Volume and Capacity of Prisms","subtitle":"From area to volume; unit cubes; prisms and their cross-sections; volume = cross-sectional area × length; cubic units, litres and capacity; composite solids; surface area compared with volume.","family":"geometry","section":{"no":3,"name":"Geometry and Measurement","strand":"Geometry Around Us","from":13,"to":20},"outcomes":["Explain volume as the number of unit cubes that fill a solid.","Identify a prism and its constant cross-section.","Find the volumes of cuboids, triangular prisms, other prisms and cylinders.","Convert between cm³, m³ and litres, and solve capacity problems.","Find the volume of composite solids and distinguish volume from surface area."],"keywords":["volume","capacity","unit cube","cuboid","prism","cross-section","cubic centimetre","cubic metre","litre","cylinder","surface area"],"notes":[{"title":"From area to volume","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**Perimeter** measures length (one dimension), **area** measures a flat surface (two dimensions), and **volume** measures the space a solid takes up (three dimensions). Volume is given in **cubic units** such as cm³ or m³."},{"k":"p","text":"To find the volume of a cuboid made of unit cubes, count the cubes in one layer and multiply by the number of layers."},{"k":"fig","id":"w20-cubes","caption":"One layer has $4\\times3=12$ cubes; two layers give $24$ cubes, so $V=4\\times3\\times2=24$ cubic units."},{"k":"p","text":"**Capacity** is the amount a container can hold. It is usually measured in litres (L) or millilitres (mL)."}],"figs":["w20-cubes"]},{"title":"Prisms and cross-sections","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **prism** is a solid with two identical, parallel end faces and the **same cross-section** all along its length. Cuboids and triangular prisms are prisms. A cylinder has a circular cross-section and is treated in the same way."},{"k":"fig","id":"w20-prism","caption":"Every slice of the prism has the same area $A$, so the volume is the area of one slice times the length."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Volume of a prism","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"V=A\\times L"},{"k":"p","text":"$A$ is the area of the cross-section and $L$ is the length of the prism (the distance between the end faces)."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w20-sections","caption":"The shaded face is the constant cross-section. Find its area first, then multiply by the length."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Special cases","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Cuboid: $V=lbh$; $\\;$ cube: $V=a^3$","Triangular prism: $V=\\tfrac{1}{2}bh\\times L$","Trapezium cross-section: $V=\\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b)h\\times L$","Cylinder: $V=\\pi r^2h$"]}]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Two different heights","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"In a triangular prism, $h$ is the height of the **triangle**, while $L$ is the **length** of the prism. Do not mix them up."}]}],"figs":["w20-prism","w20-sections"]},{"title":"Units of volume and capacity","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w20-litre","caption":"A cube of side 10 cm holds exactly 1 litre."},{"k":"table","head":["Volume","Capacity"],"rows":[["$1$ cm³","$1$ mL"],["$1000$ cm³","$1$ litre"],["$1$ m³ $=1\\,000\\,000$ cm³","$1000$ litres"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Cube the conversion factor for volume","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Since $1$ m $=100$ cm, $1$ m³ $=100\\times100\\times100=1\\,000\\,000$ cm³. Note that cm (length), cm² (area) and cm³ (volume) are different units."}]},{"k":"p","text":"Before calculating, change all lengths to the same unit. If a container is only partly full, use the depth of the liquid, or multiply the full capacity by the fraction that is filled. For capacity, use the **inside** measurements of the container."},{"k":"fig","id":"w20-tank","caption":"The water fills the tank to $\\tfrac{3}{4}$ of its depth, so its volume uses a depth of 45 cm."}],"figs":["w20-litre","w20-tank"]},{"title":"Composite solids","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Split a complicated solid into prisms that do not overlap, and **add** their volumes. If there is a hole or tunnel, **subtract** its volume. A quick method for an L-shaped solid is to find the area of the L-shaped cross-section and multiply by the length."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Surface area is different","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**Surface area** is the total area of all the faces of a solid (in cm² or m²). It tells you how much paint or wrapping is needed; volume tells you how much the solid holds."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Surface area of a cuboid","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"S=2(lb+lh+bh)"}]},{"k":"box","kind":"life","title":"Where you meet volume","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Builders order concrete in m³; water tanks, fuel tanks and buckets are measured in litres; trucks carry a fixed volume of sand per trip. When a part-load is left over, one more trip or container is needed, so round **up**."}]}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"A water tank","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A tank has inside measurements 2.4 m by 1.5 m by 1.2 m. Find its capacity in litres."}],"steps":["Use the inside measurements: $V=2.4\\times1.5\\times1.2=4.32$ m³.","$1$ m³ $=1000$ litres, so $4.32\\times1000=4320$ litres."],"answer":"4320 litres","figs":[]},{"title":"A triangular prism","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A prism has right-angled triangular ends with perpendicular sides 6 cm and 8 cm. The prism is 20 cm long. Find its volume."}],"steps":["Cross-section: $A=\\tfrac{1}{2}\\times6\\times8=24$ cm².","$V=A\\times L=24\\times20=480$ cm³."],"answer":"480 cm³","figs":[]},{"title":"A concrete beam","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A beam has a trapezium cross-section with parallel sides 0.40 m and 0.60 m, 0.30 m apart. The beam is 12 m long. Find the volume of concrete."}],"steps":["$A=\\tfrac{1}{2}(0.40+0.60)\\times0.30=0.15$ m².","$V=0.15\\times12=1.8$ m³."],"answer":"1.8 m³","figs":[]},{"title":"An L-shaped prism","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The cross-section of a prism is a 7 cm by 6 cm rectangle with a 2 cm by 3 cm rectangle cut from a corner. The prism is 15 cm long. Find its volume."}],"steps":["Cross-section: $7\\times6-2\\times3=42-6=36$ cm².","$V=36\\times15=540$ cm³."],"answer":"540 cm³","figs":[]},{"title":"Packing soap","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A box holds 48 bars of soap, each 5 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm, with no gaps. Find the total volume of the soap in cm³ and in litres."}],"steps":["One bar: $5\\times4\\times3=60$ cm³.","48 bars: $48\\times60=2880$ cm³.","$2880\\div1000=2.88$ litres."],"answer":"2880 cm³ $=2.88$ litres","figs":[]},{"title":"A partly filled fish tank","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A fish tank is 120 cm long, 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep inside. It is filled to $\\tfrac{3}{4}$ of its depth. Find the volume of water in litres."}],"steps":["Depth of water: $\\tfrac{3}{4}\\times60=45$ cm.","$V=120\\times50\\times45=270\\,000$ cm³.","$270\\,000\\div1000=270$ litres."],"answer":"270 litres","figs":[]},{"title":"Trucks of soil","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A trench is 16 m long, 2.5 m wide and 0.8 m deep. A truck carries at most 6 m³ of soil. How many truckloads are needed?"}],"steps":["Volume of soil: $16\\times2.5\\times0.8=32$ m³.","$32\\div6=5\\tfrac{1}{3}$.","Five loads carry only 30 m³, so a sixth load is needed for the last 2 m³."],"answer":"6 truckloads","figs":[]},{"title":"From volume to surface area","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A cuboid has a volume of 1440 cm³, a length of 12 cm and a breadth of 10 cm. Find its height and its total surface area."}],"steps":["$V=lbh$: $1440=12\\times10\\times h=120h$, so $h=12$ cm.","$S=2(lb+lh+bh)=2(120+144+120)=2\\times384=768$ cm²."],"answer":"Height 12 cm; surface area 768 cm².","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results for Week 20","items":["Prism: $V=A\\times L$ (cross-sectional area × length).","Cuboid $V=lbh$; cube $V=a^3$; cylinder $V=\\pi r^2h$.","$1$ litre $=1000$ cm³; $\\;1$ m³ $=1000$ litres $=1\\,000\\,000$ cm³.","Composite solids: add the parts, subtract holes.","Cuboid surface area: $S=2(lb+lh+bh)$."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"A cuboid measures 6 cm by 5 cm by 4 cm. Its volume is","options":["15 cm³","120 cm³","60 cm³","90 cm³"],"correct":1,"explain":"$6\\times5\\times4=120$ cm³."},{"q":"A prism has a cross-sectional area of 18 cm² and a length of 9 cm. Find its volume.","options":["162 cm³","27 cm³","54 cm³","81 cm³"],"correct":0,"explain":"$V=A\\times L=18\\times9=162$ cm³."},{"q":"How many litres are there in 1 m³?","options":["10","100","10 000","1000"],"correct":3,"explain":"$1$ m³ $=1000$ litres."},{"q":"The volume of a cube of side 7 cm is","options":["49 cm³","21 cm³","343 cm³","28 cm³"],"correct":2,"explain":"$7^3=343$ cm³."},{"q":"A tank holds 2.5 m³ of water. How many litres is this?","options":["250 L","2500 L","25 L","25 000 L"],"correct":1,"explain":"$2.5\\times1000=2500$ litres."},{"q":"A prism has a cross-section of 24 cm² and a volume of 600 cm³. How long is it?","options":["25 cm","144 cm","576 cm","24 cm"],"correct":0,"explain":"$L=600\\div24=25$ cm."},{"q":"How many 2 m³ containers are needed to hold 7 m³?","options":["3","7","2","4"],"correct":3,"explain":"$7\\div2=3.5$, so 4 containers are needed."},{"q":"Which unit is used for volume?","options":["cm","cm²","cm³","degrees"],"correct":2,"explain":"Volume has three dimensions, so it is measured in cubic units."},{"q":"A prism has a 10 cm² cross-section and a length of 30 cm. A hole of 5 cm³ is drilled out. What volume is left?","options":["300 cm³","295 cm³","305 cm³","150 cm³"],"correct":1,"explain":"$10\\times30-5=295$ cm³."},{"q":"A trapezium cross-section has parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm and height 4 cm. Its area is","options":["64 cm²","16 cm²","40 cm²","32 cm²"],"correct":3,"explain":"$\\tfrac{1}{2}(6+10)\\times4=32$ cm²."}],"exercise":[{"q":"A tank has inside measurements 2.8 m by 1.5 m by 0.9 m and is $60\\%$ full. How many litres of water does it hold?","a":"$2.8\\times1.5\\times0.9=3.78$ m³; $60\\%$ of that is $2.268$ m³ $=2268$ litres."},{"q":"A gutter is a triangular prism with a triangle of base 40 cm and height 25 cm, and it is 3 m long. Find its volume in litres.","a":"$A=\\tfrac{1}{2}\\times40\\times25=500$ cm²; $V=500\\times300=150\\,000$ cm³ $=150$ litres."},{"q":"A prism is 20 cm long. Its cross-section is a 9 cm by 8 cm rectangle with a 3 cm by 4 cm notch cut out. Find its volume.","a":"$(72-12)\\times20=1200$ cm³"},{"q":"How many sandbags of 0.75 m³ are needed to store 14 m³ of sand?","a":"$14\\div0.75=18.7$, so 19 bags."},{"q":"A cube and a cuboid both have a volume of 216 cm³. Find the side of the cube and give three whole-number measurements for the cuboid.","a":"Cube side 6 cm; for example $12\\times6\\times3$ or $9\\times8\\times3$ cm."},{"q":"Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 7 cm and height 10 cm, using $\\pi=\\dfrac{22}{7}$. Give the answer in litres too.","a":"$\\dfrac{22}{7}\\times49\\times10=1540$ cm³ $=1.54$ litres."},{"q":"Write 3.5 m³ in cm³.","a":"$3.5\\times1\\,000\\,000=3\\,500\\,000$ cm³"},{"q":"Find the total surface area of a cube of side 5 cm.","a":"$6\\times5^2=150$ cm²"}],"theory":[{"q":"Explain why the volume of a prism is its cross-sectional area times its length.","steps":["A prism is made of identical slices, each with the same area $A$.","Like layers of unit cubes, the slices are stacked along the whole length $L$.","So the total space is $A\\times L$ cubic units."],"answer":"$V=A\\times L$, just as volume = (cubes in one layer) × (number of layers).","model":null},{"q":"A tank measures 1.8 m by 1.4 m by 0.9 m inside. The top 20 cm is empty. How many litres of water does it contain?","steps":["Depth of water: $0.9-0.2=0.7$ m.","$V=1.8\\times1.4\\times0.7=1.764$ m³.","$1.764\\times1000=1764$ litres."],"answer":"1764 litres","model":null},{"q":"A triangular prism has a triangle of base 12 cm and height 5 cm, and the prism is 30 cm long. Find its volume.","steps":["$A=\\tfrac{1}{2}\\times12\\times5=30$ cm².","$V=30\\times30=900$ cm³."],"answer":"900 cm³","model":null},{"q":"A solid is a 10 cm by 6 cm by 4 cm cuboid with a rectangular tunnel 3 cm by 2 cm running through its 4 cm thickness. Find its volume.","steps":["Cuboid: $10\\times6\\times4=240$ cm³.","Tunnel: $3\\times2\\times4=24$ cm³.","Solid: $240-24=216$ cm³."],"answer":"216 cm³","model":null},{"q":"Explain why a 2 m³ tank cannot hold 20 000 litres.","steps":["$1$ m³ $=1000$ litres, so $2$ m³ $=2000$ litres.","20 000 litres would need 20 m³.","The mistake is using a factor of 10 000 instead of 1000."],"answer":"The tank holds only 2000 litres.","model":null}],"checklist":["I can explain volume as the number of unit cubes in a solid.","I can identify the cross-section of a prism and use $V=A\\times L$.","I can find volumes of cuboids, triangular prisms and cylinders.","I can convert between cm³, m³ and litres.","I can find the volume of composite solids and solve capacity problems.","I can tell surface area from volume."],"plan":{"lessons":[[{"j":0,"notes":true,"exs":[0]},{"j":1,"notes":true,"exs":[1,2,3]}],[{"j":2,"notes":true,"exs":[4,5]},{"j":3,"notes":true,"exs":[]},{"j":4,"notes":true,"exs":[6,7]}]],"exSec":[0,1,1,1,2,2,4,4],"quizSec":[0,1,0,2,4,1,4,0,1,1],"exerSec":[2,1,1,4,2,1,0,4],"thSec":[1,2,1,3,4],"sumSec":[1,1,2,3,4],"chkSec":[0,1,1,1,3,4],"weights":[1301.95,3669.5,2602.45,260.25,2170.8],"figs":[{"id":"w20-cubes","sec":0,"lesson":1,"caption":"One layer has $4\\times3=12$ cubes; <script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w21">{"year":1,"week":21,"id":"y1w21","title":"Understanding Data and Methods of Data Collection","subtitle":"Data and statistics; population and sample; quantitative (discrete and continuous) and qualitative (nominal and ordinal) data; primary and secondary data; questionnaires, interviews, observation and records; fair sampling and ethics.","family":"data","section":{"no":4,"name":"Data and Probability","strand":"Making Sense of and Using Data","from":21,"to":24},"outcomes":["Explain what data and statistics are, and write a clear statistical question.","Distinguish a population from a sample, and a census from a sample survey.","Classify data as discrete, continuous, nominal or ordinal, and as primary or secondary.","Choose and justify a suitable method of collecting data, and write neutral survey questions.","Select a fair sample, including a proportionate stratified sample, and handle data ethically."],"keywords":["data","statistics","variable","population","sample","census","quantitative","qualitative","discrete","continuous","nominal","ordinal","primary data","secondary data","questionnaire","bias","stratified sample"],"notes":[{"title":"Data and statistics","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**Data** are facts, counts, measurements or descriptions collected to answer a question. **Statistics** is the work of collecting, organising, analysing and interpreting data."},{"k":"p","text":"Good work starts with a **clear question**. “How long do Year 1 learners take to travel to school?” is clear; “What about travel?” is not. Decide exactly which **variable** you will record and how you will measure it."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Population, sample and variable","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Key terms","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["The **population** is the whole group you want to find out about, for example all 1,200 learners in a school.","A **sample** is a smaller group chosen from the population.","A **census** collects data from every member of the population.","A **variable** is a characteristic that can differ from person to person (height, transport, age); each recorded value is an **observation**."]}]},{"k":"p","text":"How the sample is chosen matters as much as its size. Asking only the first 20 learners at the gate may leave out learners who travel far or arrive late."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Types of data","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w21-types","caption":"Quantitative data are numbers (counted or measured); qualitative data are categories (unordered or ranked)."},{"k":"table","head":["Type","Meaning","Examples"],"rows":[["Discrete","counted; usually whole numbers","number of siblings, books, absentees"],["Continuous","measured; any value in a range","height, mass, time, temperature"],["Nominal","categories with no order","favourite subject, transport, colour"],["Ordinal","categories with a natural order","poor/fair/good, 1st/2nd/3rd"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Numbers that are not quantities","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A phone number or a learner’s ID number is made of digits, but it is a **label**, not a quantity: it makes no sense to find its average. Coding categories as 1 = bus and 2 = bicycle does not turn transport into quantitative data."}]}],"figs":["w21-types"]},{"title":"Primary and secondary data","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Primary data** are collected by you for your own study: surveys, interviews, observations or experiments.","**Secondary data** already exist: school registers, census reports, newspapers or websites."]},{"k":"p","text":"Before using secondary data, check the **source**, the **date**, the **definitions** used and whether the data are **complete**."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Methods of collecting data","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w21-methods","caption":"Four common ways to collect data."},{"k":"ul","items":["**Questionnaire:** many people answer the same written questions. Multiple-choice items are quick to count; open questions give reasons.","**Interview:** questions asked face to face. You can follow up answers, but it takes time and the interviewer can influence replies.","**Observation:** watch and record events with a checklist or tally, for example vehicles passing a gate.","**Existing records:** registers, receipts or reports (secondary data), used with permission."]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Avoid leading questions","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"“Don’t you agree the canteen is too expensive?” pushes people towards one answer. Ask instead: “How would you rate the canteen prices: very low, low, fair, high, very high?” Try your questions on a few people first (a **pilot**) to find unclear wording."}]}],"figs":["w21-methods"]},{"title":"Sampling fairly","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Simple random sample:** every member has the same chance of being chosen, for example names drawn from the register.","**Stratified sample:** the population is split into groups (strata) and each group is sampled in proportion to its size.","**Convenience sample:** whoever is easiest to reach. It is quick but often **biased**."]},{"k":"fig","id":"w21-sampling","caption":"A random sample (left) and a stratified sample (right) that keeps the proportions of girls and boys."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Proportionate stratified sample","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Number to choose from a group:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\frac{\\text{group size}}{\\text{population size}}\\times\\text{sample size}"}]},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Ethics","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Take part only with consent; do not collect names or private information unless they are really needed; keep answers confidential; and report results honestly."}]}],"figs":["w21-sampling"]},{"title":"Data quality","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Before analysing, check that all values use the **same units**, that no answers are missing, and that categories do not overlap (for example “0–5 km” and “5–10 km” overlap at 5). Good graphs cannot repair badly collected data. In Week 22 we organise data into tables and graphs."}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"Classifying variables","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A class survey records each learner’s height, age in completed years, favourite subject and satisfaction (low, medium, high). Classify each variable."}],"steps":["Height is measured and can take decimal values: quantitative, **continuous**.","Age in completed years is a whole number: quantitative, **discrete**.","Favourite subject has no order: qualitative, **nominal**.","Satisfaction has an order (low $<$ medium $<$ high): qualitative, **ordinal**."],"answer":"Continuous; discrete; nominal; ordinal.","figs":[]},{"title":"Is the sample fair?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A researcher wants the average travel time of all 900 learners in a school. She asks the first 30 learners who arrive. Name the population and the sample, and comment on the method."}],"steps":["Population: all 900 learners. Sample: the 30 early arrivals.","This is a convenience sample.","Early arrivals may live closer or use faster transport, so the result may be biased.","Better: choose learners at random from the school register, or stratify by community."],"answer":"Population 900, sample 30; the convenience sample is likely to be biased.","figs":[]},{"title":"Codes are not quantities","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A school records shoe sizes using the codes 1, 2, 3 and 4 for four size groups. Is it sensible to find the mean of the codes?"}],"steps":["The codes stand for ordered size groups, not amounts.","The gaps between the groups may not be equal, so arithmetic on the codes has no clear meaning.","To calculate an average, record the actual shoe sizes instead."],"answer":"No. The codes are ordinal labels; record real sizes if you need a mean.","figs":[]},{"title":"Watching a queue","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"To study lunch queues, a learner counts how many people join the canteen line in each 5-minute interval for one hour. Name the method and the type of data, and give one limitation."}],"steps":["Method: direct, structured observation.","The counts are quantitative, discrete data; there are $60\\div5=12$ intervals.","One hour on one day may not represent other days.","Improvement: repeat on several days at the same times."],"answer":"Observation; discrete data; one day may not be typical.","figs":[]},{"title":"A stratified sample","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A school has 600 learners: 360 girls and 240 boys. Choose a proportionate stratified sample of 50."}],"steps":["Girls: $\\dfrac{360}{600}\\times50=0.6\\times50=30$.","Boys: $\\dfrac{240}{600}\\times50=0.4\\times50=20$.","Check: $30+20=50$ ✓. Choose randomly within each group."],"answer":"30 girls and 20 boys","figs":[]},{"title":"Fixing a biased question","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A questionnaire asks: “Since online lessons are better than classroom lessons, which do you prefer?” Explain the problem and rewrite the question."}],"steps":["The first part states an opinion as a fact, which leads people to one answer.","Neutral version: “Which kind of lesson do you prefer: online, classroom, a mixture, or no preference?”","Add an optional question asking for reasons."],"answer":"Remove the leading statement and give balanced choices.","figs":[]},{"title":"Secondary records","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A canteen manager uses last year’s payment records to estimate spending this year. What kind of data is this, and what two checks should be made?"}],"steps":["The records already exist, so they are **secondary** data.","Check that prices and buying habits have not changed much since last year.","Check that the records are complete (for example, no missing cash payments)."],"answer":"Secondary data; check that they are up to date and complete.","figs":[]},{"title":"Mixed units","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A learner records 12 classroom temperatures, some in °C and some in °F. How should the data be cleaned?"}],"steps":["Find the unit of every reading.","Convert the °F readings using $C=(F-32)\\times\\dfrac{5}{9}$; for example $86^\\circ\\text{F}=(86-32)\\times\\dfrac{5}{9}=30^\\circ\\text{C}$.","Record all values in °C (keeping the original readings), and only then calculate averages."],"answer":"Convert every reading to the same unit before any analysis.","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results for Week 21","items":["Population: the whole group. units."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"A learner’s mass of 52.4 kg is an example of","options":["discrete quantitative data","continuous quantitative data","nominal data","ordinal data"],"correct":1,"explain":"Mass data"],"correct":0,"explain":"Absentees are counted in whole numbers."},{"q":"Which variable is nominal?","options":["position in a test","temperature","preferred way of travelling to chosen."},{"q":"Which method is best for counting vehicles passing the school gate?","options":["an unstructured opinion interview","an observation tally","a favourite-subject questionnaire","reading old articles only"],"correct":1,"explain":"Watching and tallying records the vehicles directly."},{"q":"Why must readings in °C and °F be changed to one unit?","options":["to increase the sample units."}],"exercise":[{"q":"Write a five-question survey on how learners travel to school and how long it takes. (nominal)"},{"q":"A school has 480 boarders and 320 day learners. <script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w22">{"year":1,"week":22,"id":"y1w22","title":"Organising and Presenting Data; Mean, Median and Mode","subtitle":"Frequency tables and grouped data; bar charts, pie charts, histograms and line graphs; the mean, median and mode; the range and the effect of outliers; using a spreadsheet.","family":"data","section":{"no":4,"name":"Data and Probability","strand":"Making Sense of and Using Data","from":21,"to":24},"outcomes":["Organise raw data into ungrouped and grouped frequency tables.","Draw and read bar charts, pie charts, histograms and line graphs, and spot misleading graphs.","Calculate the mean, median, mode and range, including from frequency tables.","Estimate the mean of grouped data using class midpoints.","Choose the most suitable average and explain the effect of outliers."],"keywords":["raw data","frequency table","relative frequency","class interval","midpoint","bar chart","pie chart","histogram","line graph","mean","median","mode","range","outlier"],"notes":[{"title":"From raw data to a frequency table","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**Raw data** are the observations as they were collected. Twelve learners give the number of books they read in a month:"},{"k":"math","tex":"1,\\ 3,\\ 2,\\ 1,\\ 4,\\ 2,\\ 3,\\ 2,\\ 1,\\ 5,\\ 2,\\ 4"},{"k":"p","text":"It is hard to see the pattern. A **frequency table** groups equal values and counts them (tally marks in groups of five make counting easy):"},{"k":"table","head":["Books read, $x$","1","2","3","4","5","Total"],"rows":[["Frequency, $f$","3","4","2","2","1","12"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Always check the total","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The frequencies must add up to the number of observations: $3+4+2+2+1=12$ ✓."}]},{"k":"p","text":"The **relative frequency** of a value is $\\dfrac{\\text{frequency}}{\\text{total}}$; multiply by $100\\%$ to get a percentage. For example, 2 books has relative frequency $\\dfrac{4}{12}=\\dfrac{1}{3}\\approx33\\%$."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Grouped data","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"When there are many different values, group them into **class intervals** such as $0$–$9$, $10$–$19$, $20$–$29$. The classes must not overlap, and every value must fit in exactly one class."},{"k":"ul","items":["The **class width** of $10$–$19$ is $10$.","The **midpoint** is the average of the class limits: $\\dfrac{10+19}{2}=14.5$."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Presenting data","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w22-bar","caption":"A bar chart compares categories or separate values. The bars have gaps and start from zero."},{"k":"fig","id":"w22-pie","caption":"A pie chart shows how a whole is shared. Each member of the club is worth $9^\\circ$."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Pie chart angles","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"\\text{sector angle}=\\frac{\\text{frequency}}{\\text{total frequency}}\\times360^\\circ"},{"k":"p","text":"The angles must add up to $360^\\circ$."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w22-histogram","caption":"A histogram shows grouped numerical data. The bars touch because the classes follow on from each other."},{"k":"fig","id":"w22-line","caption":"A line graph shows how a quantity changes over time."},{"k":"table","head":["Graph","Best used for"],"rows":[["Bar chart","comparing categories (bars with gaps)"],["Pie chart","parts of a whole"],["Histogram","grouped numerical data (bars touching)"],["Line graph","change over time"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Honest graphs","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Give every graph a title, labelled axes with units, an even scale and a key if needed. A bar chart’s axis should start at **zero**; otherwise the bars’ lengths mislead. Avoid 3-D effects that distort the sizes."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w22-axis","caption":"The same club sizes drawn two ways. Starting the axis at 10 hides clubs B and D and exaggerates the differences."}],"figs":["w22-bar","w22-pie","w22-histogram","w22-line","w22-axis"]},{"title":"The three averages","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Mean, median and mode","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Mean:** $\\bar{x}=\\dfrac{\\text{sum of the values}}{\\text{number of values}}=\\dfrac{\\sum x}{n}$","**Mean from a frequency table:** $\\bar{x}=\\dfrac{\\sum fx}{\\sum f}$","**Median:** the middle value when the data are in order. For $n$ values it is the $\\left(\\dfrac{n+1}{2}\\right)$th value; if $n$ is even, it is the mean of the two middle values.","**Mode:** the value that occurs most often. There may be one mode, more than one, or none."]}]},{"k":"p","text":"For grouped data, use the class **midpoints** as $x$ in $\\dfrac{\\sum fx}{\\sum f}$. The answer is an **estimate**, because we do not know the exact values inside each class."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Range, outliers and choosing an average","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **range** is the largest value minus the smallest value. It measures the spread but depends only on the two extremes."},{"k":"p","text":"An **outlier** is a value far from the rest. It pulls the mean towards it but hardly moves the median."},{"k":"fig","id":"w22-outlier","caption":"Eight fares are between GH₵5 and GH₵9, but one is GH₵44. The median (7) describes a typical fare better than the mean (11.11)."},{"k":"table","head":["Average","Strength","Use it when…"],"rows":[["Mean","uses every value","the data have no extreme values"],["Median","not affected by outliers","there are extreme values, e.g. incomes or fares"],["Mode","works for categories too","you want the most popular item, e.g. a shoe size"]]}],"figs":["w22-outlier"]},{"title":"Using a spreadsheet","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"In a spreadsheet, `SUM` adds values, `AVERAGE` gives the mean, `MEDIAN` gives the median, `MODE.SNGL` gives a single mode and `COUNT` counts the numbers. Check a few results by hand, and make sure blank cells are not being counted as zeros."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Reporting results","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"State who was measured, when, the units, and whether the data come from a sample. A correct calculation is not automatically a correct conclusion."}]}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"A frequency table and the mode","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A teacher records the library visits of 15 learners in a month: $2,1,3,2,4,2,1,5,3,2,4,1,3,2,3$. Make a frequency table and find the mode."}],"steps":["Values in order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.","Count: 1 visit: 3; 2 visits: 5; 3 visits: 4; 4 visits: 2; 5 visits: 1.","Check: $3+5+4+2+1=15$ ✓.","The highest frequency is 5, for 2 visits."],"answer":"Mode $=2$ visits (see the bar chart in the notes).","figs":[]},{"title":"Mean, median, mode and range","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The scores of six learners are $9,\\ 11,\\ 13,\\ 13,\\ 14,\\ 18$. Find the mean, median, mode and range. Which measure uses all six values?"}],"steps":["Sum: $9+11+13+13+14+18=78$, so the mean is $78\\div6=13$.","Six values: the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th values, $\\dfrac{13+13}{2}=13$.","Mode: $13$ (it occurs twice).","Range: $18-9=9$."],"answer":"Mean 13, median 13, mode 13, range 9. The mean uses all six values.","figs":[]},{"title":"Angles for a pie chart","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"40 club members chose their favourite sport: football 18, athletics 10, volleyball 8, basketball 4. Find the angle for each sector."}],"steps":["Each member is worth $360^\\circ\\div40=9^\\circ$.","Football $18\\times9^\\circ=162^\\circ$; athletics $10\\times9^\\circ=90^\\circ$.","Volleyball $8\\times9^\\circ=72^\\circ$; basketball $4\\times9^\\circ=36^\\circ$.","Check: $162+90+72+36=360$ ✓."],"answer":"$162^\\circ$, $90^\\circ$, $72^\\circ$, $36^\\circ$","figs":[]},{"title":"Mean of grouped data","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Daily sales of exercise books: $0$–$9$: 3 days; $10$–$19$: 5 days; $20$–$29$: 9 days; $30$–$39$: 3 days. Find the mean and the median, and decide which better describes a typical fare."}],"steps":["Sum $=100$, so the mean is $100\\div9\\approx11.11$.","The 5th of the nine ordered values is the median: $7$.","The fare of GH₵44 is an outlier and pulls the mean up."],"answer":"Mean $\\approx$ GH₵11.11; median GH₵7. The median is more typical.","figs":[]},{"title":"Reading a pie chart","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"In a pie chart of 120 learners, the sector for learners who walk to school is $54^\\circ$. Find $x$ and the median."}],"steps":["Total $=7\\times6=42$.","The known values add to $30$, so $x=42-30=12$.","In order: $2,4,6,8,10,12$. What is wrong, and how should it be drawn?"}],"steps":["Club D (5) and club B (8) are below 10, so their bars disappear.","Cutting the axis also makes A and C look much more different than they are.","Start the axis at 0 with an even scale (0, 5, 10, 15), label the axes and draw equal-width bars with gaps."],"answer":"The axis must start at zero; see the corrected chart in the notes.","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results for Week 22","items":["Frequencies must add up to the total; relative frequency $=\\dfrac{f}{\\text{total}}$.","Midpoint of a class $=\\dfrac{\\text{lower}+\\text{upper}}{2}$.","Pie chart angle $=\\dfrac{f}{\\text{total}}\\times360^\\circ$.","Mean $=\\dfrac{\\sum x}{n}$ or $\\dfrac{\\sum fx}{\\sum f}$; median $=$ middle value; mode $=$ most frequent.","Range $=$ largest $-$ smallest; outliers affect the mean far more than the median."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"What is the mode of $2,2,3,4,4,4,6$?","options":["$2$","$3$","$4$","$6$"],"correct":2,"explain":"$4$ occurs three times, more than any other value."},{"q":"The mean of $6,8,10,12$ is","options":["$8$","$9$","$10$","$12$"],"correct":1,"explain":"Sum $=36$; $36\\div4=9$."},{"q":"The median of $4,7,9,11,14,16$ is","options":["$9$","$10$","$11$","$12$"],"correct":1,"explain":"The two middle values are 9 and 11: $\\dfrac{9+11}{2}=10$."},{"q":"A pie-chart sector of $90^\\circ$ is what fraction of the whole?","options":["$\\dfrac{1}{2}$","$\\dfrac{1}{3}$","$\\dfrac{1}{4}$","$\\dfrac{1}{5}$"],"correct":2,"explain":"$\\dfrac{90}{360}=\\dfrac{1}{4}$."},{"q":"The values 1, 2 and 3 have frequencies 3, 5 and 2. What percentage is this?","options":["$15\\%$","$20\\%$","$40\\%$","$25\\%$"],"correct":3,"explain":"$\\dfrac{15}{60}\\times100\\%=25\\%$."},{"q":"Which graph is best for showing a temperature recorded every hour?","options":["a pie chart","a line graph","a pictogram","a table of labels"],"correct":1,"explain":"A line graph shows change over time."},{"q":"The midpoint of the class $20$–$29$ is","options":["20","25","24.5","29"],"correct":2,"explain":"$\\dfrac{20+29}{2}=24.5$."}],"exercise":[{"q":"Marks: $6,8,7,6,9,10,8,6,7,9,8,6$. Midpoints stand in for the unknown exact ages."},{"q":"Daily attendance: 210, 211, 212, 210, 250. Which is more typical of an ordinary day, the mean or the median?","a":"Mean $=218.6$, median $=211$. The median, because 250 is an unusual day."},{"q":"Find the mean of: $x=1,2,3,4$ with $f=2,5,8,5$.","a":"$\\sum fx=2+10+24+20=56$, $\\sum f=20$, mean $=2.8$."},{"q":"The mean of five numbers is 12. The conclusions often lead to a new, sharper question."},{"k":"p","text":"The plan states the **population**, a manageable **sample**, the **method** of collecting data, how the data will be organised, and what will be compared."}],"figs":["w23-cycle"]},{"title":"Populations, samples and bias","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **population** is the whole group the conclusion is about; the **sample** is the members actually studied. A sample chosen for convenience can be **biased**: interviewing only learners who arrive very early will under-represent long journeys."},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Fairer samples","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Choose learners at random from a complete class list, or take a stratified sample from every class and every type of transport. Never claim results for the whole country after studying one classroom."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Collecting data ethically","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Use short, neutral questions, and state the units (minutes, cedis, kilometres).","Ask for consent; do not record names or private details unless they are really needed.","Try the questions on a few classmates first (a pilot survey).","Check each value when it is recorded. Record missing answers as **missing**, not as zero."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"From raw data to evidence","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Before calculating, **clean** the data: remove duplicates, check impossible values (a journey of 900 minutes?), add missing units and make category names consistent. Then:"},{"k":"ol","items":["make a clear table and a suitable chart;","state the sample size $n$;","calculate a suitable average **and** a measure of spread (such as the range);","explain what the numbers mean in everyday words."]},{"k":"fig","id":"w23-travel","caption":"How 40 learners travel to school. Giving the counts, the percentages and $n$ makes the chart easy to check."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"One number is not enough","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Two groups can have the same mean but very different ranges. Report an average together with a measure of spread, and mention unusual values instead of hiding them."}]}],"figs":["w23-travel"]},{"title":"Comparing groups fairly","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"When groups have different sizes, compare **percentages (rates)**, not just counts."},{"k":"math","tex":"\\text{rate}=\\frac{\\text{number with the feature}}{\\text{group size}}\\times100\\%"},{"k":"fig","id":"w23-rates","caption":"Class B has more passes and more learners. Its pass rate is 4 percentage points higher."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Association is not causation","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"If learners who live farther away are late more often, distance may be **associated** with lateness, but it is not proved to be the **cause**: weather, departure time and road conditions may matter too. A before-and-after comparison does not prove that a change caused the difference."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w23-water","caption":"Water use fell by 20% after the taps were repaired, but other things may also have changed."}],"figs":["w23-rates","w23-water"]},{"title":"Writing the report","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w23-report","caption":"A complete one-page report."},{"k":"p","text":"A complete report has: a **title**; the **question and purpose**; the **population, sample and method**; a **table and chart** (numbered and labelled); the **calculations**; the **findings**; the **limitations**; **recommendations** linked to the findings; and a **conclusion**."}],"figs":["w23-report"]},{"title":"Observation and inference","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"“14 of the 20 learners surveyed travel for more than 30 minutes” is an **observation** about the sample. “Most learners in Ghana travel for more than 30 minutes” is an **inference** that these data cannot support."},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Presenting your project","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"State clearly what you observed and what you are inferring. Invite questions about the sample, the calculations, the scales of the charts and other possible explanations, and be ready to change a conclusion if new data do not support it."}]}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"A biased sample","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A committee samples 25 of the school’s 500 learners by interviewing only those in the library at 7 a.m. Explain the problem and suggest a better method."}],"steps":["The population is all 500 learners.","Early library users may differ from late arrivals and from learners who never use the library.","Results from them cannot safely be applied to every learner.","Better: choose random numbers from the full school roll, or stratify by year group and class, and record the method and any non-responses."],"answer":"The sample is likely to be biased; use random or stratified sampling from a complete list.","figs":[]},{"title":"Percentages for a chart","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A class survey of 40 respondents finds: walk 18, taxi 12, bus 10. Give each as a relative frequency and a percentage, and suggest a chart."}],"steps":["Check: $18+12+10=40$ ✓.","Walk $\\dfrac{18}{40}=0.45=45\\%$; taxi $\\dfrac{12}{40}=0.30=30\\%$; bus $\\dfrac{10}{40}=0.25=25\\%$.","Check: $45\\%+30\\%+25\\%=100\\%$ ✓.","A bar chart compares the categories clearly; a pie chart also shows the parts of the whole."],"answer":"45%, 30%, 25%; a labelled bar chart.","figs":[]},{"title":"Comparing pass rates","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Class A: 18 of 30 learners pass.
